zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical review aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The supplied page subset was consulted after independent scan reading for lexical and coverage comparison. Corrections and English comments are reviewer-authored; this copy's printed forms are determined from its scan.

lines.note: Nuicucumi is nuikukumi, sewing over or enclosing something in a sewn covering. The Portuguese begins “sew over, leaving”; the printed headword has m, and deixã- continues on the next physical line.

runs.text: do dentro algũa couſa, como bainha de fora que

lines.note: The enclosed object remains inside, as with an outer sheath. This continues the definition rather than introducing another entry; the nasal abbreviation in algũa is retained.

runs.text: ſe coſe ſobre a outra bainha mais interior da eſ-

lines.note: The outer sheath is sewn over the other, inner sheath of the sword. The scan reads outra, not the OCR's ouira; eſ- continues as pada below.
Pada completes eſpada, “sword,” and closes the example of a sewn outer covering. It is a genuine short continuation row, not furniture.
Nuicucumizaya names the sewn outer scabbard-cover just described. The Portuguese says an outer sheath used for a purpose continued below; the printed pa- is retained.

runs.text: ra reſguardo da outra principal da Catana.

lines.note: The covering protects the sword's main scabbard. Catana is a Japanese loanword embedded in the Portuguese explanation, not a new Japanese example.
Nuifacu is nuihaku, textile decoration combining embroidery and gold work. Here bastidor denotes the embroidered work, with interspersed gold ornament; entre- joins ſachados below.
This completes entreſachados, describing the gold decoration interspersed in the embroidered work. The long initial ſ belongs to the Portuguese continuation, not a new headword.
Nuimono means needlework or embroidery. Both the missing i in the headword and broslado in the Portuguese are visible; broslado is the historical word for embroidered work, not the OCR's broclado.

runs.text: Brosladores, ou caſa õde ſe faz

lines.note: Nuimonoya denotes embroiderers or their workshop. Brosladores is retained in its printed historical spelling; the explanation continues with what is made there.
The workshop makes bastidor, embroidered work in this context. This short row finishes Nuimonoya and remains attached to that entry.

runs.text: Fio, ou linhas por torcer feitas de linho

lines.note: Nuiſo denotes sewing fibre or thread; the Portuguese specifies thread not yet twisted, made from the material completed below. The long ſ in the headword is retained.
Canemo completes linho canemo, hemp fibre. It identifies the material of the untwisted sewing thread rather than giving a separate Japanese term.
Nuitate, nuitatsuru, nuitateta means to finish sewing or making up a garment. The historical tçuru ending is printed and should not be replaced with a modern conjugation.
This finishes the alternative explanation “to make a garment, etc.” The existing short-s transcription of vestido is retained where the st ligature does not warrant an allograph change.
Nuitçuqe, nuitsukeru, means to attach by sewing. Vt introduces the example on the next line and is part of the italic Portuguese apparatus.
The example says that many jewels were sewn onto a garment: isho ni amata no shugyoku o nuitsuketari. The final caron in Ixǒ and the historical x spelling are retained.

The citation reads Part. 1. Goſag.; the initial is G, not the OCR's C. The translation begins “by sewing, attached many stones.” The abbreviated source label is retained without a speculative expansion.
These are precious stones attached to the garment, completing the preceding example's translation. The line is Portuguese throughout.
Numa is a marsh or bog; the Portuguese gives a mire or muddy place. This begins a new entry after the sewing vocabulary.
Numameqi describes a thing being smooth or sleek. The Portuguese starts with liſa, “smooth,” and the printed historical form is retained rather than regularized to a different modern word.
Nedea adds “sleek” or “smooth” to liſa, completing the definition of Numameqi. No new headword is present.

Numarito and the alternative numerito are adverbial expressions for a smooth or slippery manner. The visibly spaced Num arito in the example is retained as supplied, and numeri- continues below; V introduces the illustration.
This completes numerito xite, an alternative to numarito xite. Adu. Idem identifies an adverb with the same sense as the preceding smoothness entry.

runs.text: Peça, ouſeda tecida de hũa ſoo cor ſem

lines.note: Nume is a piece of plain, single-coloured silk fabric. The Portuguese explains that it is woven in one colour, continuing below with the absence of decoration; the printed joining ouſeda is retained.
The cloth has neither decorative work nor stripes. This completes the definition of the fabric, not the preceding smoothness vocabulary.
Numeracaxi, numerakasu, means to make something slip. The causative sense agrees with fazer eſcorregar; aita is a historical inflection and is not an OCR error to modernize.
Numeri means to slip, with Suberi recommended as the better expression by Meliùs. Suberi is thus a Japanese word within the dictionary's explanatory apparatus. Eſ- continues as corregar below.

runs.text: corregar. ¶ Item, Ser algũa couſa liſa,

lines.note: The first sense is “slip”; a second sense is for a thing to be smooth. The paragraph sign separates senses within Numeri, not separate entries.
The second sense adds “and somewhat slippery.” Como qualifies the description rather than introducing a concrete example.

This is a plant name, explained only as “an herb so called.” Enlargement shows an abraded final u with a distinct caron, giving Numeribiǔ rather than the OCR's Numeribin; no botanical identification is supplied by the text.
Numerito refers the reader back to Numarito, where the alternative adverbial forms were given. Numarito is a Japanese cross-reference inside the Latin-Portuguese apparatus.
Nuno is cloth, here specified as fabric made of hemp. The entry's material-specific explanation is retained rather than broadened silently to all modern senses of nuno.

runs.text: Vestido de linho canemo cõ borra.

lines.note: Nunoco is a padded garment made of hemp cloth; cõ borra specifies the stuffing or wadding. The historical spelling with c is retained.

runs.text: Caſa onde fazem, ou vẽdem nonos.

lines.note: Nunoya is a place where cloth is made or sold. The embedded loanword is visibly nonos, a Portuguese plural, not an instruction to change the Japanese headword Nuno.

runs.text: Paßar, ou ſair de parte a

lines.note: Nuqe, nukeru, first means to pass or come out through something. The phrase de parte a parte continues onto the next row and means from one side to the other.
A second sense is to come loose or be withdrawn. The scan retains the anomalous doubled initial Aa in Aarrancarſe; the ending is rſe, not the OCR's sfe. The spelling is not silently normalized.

runs.text: como prègo, ou eſpada q̃ ſe deſem bainha porſi.

lines.note: Examples are a nail that comes out or a sword that leaves its sheath by itself. The abbreviation q̃, the grave in prègo, and the supplied separation deſem bainha are retained.

runs.text: &c. ¶ Item, per met. Eſcapulir, ou a-

lines.note: A further, explicitly metaphorical sense is to slip away or escape. The terminal a- belongs to acolherſe on the next physical row.
The metaphorical example concerns someone escaping from confinement. A new example then begins Yu-, which must be read with qinuquru below rather than as a separate word.
Yuqinuquru, begun above, means to go past others while walking. The Portuguese an- continues as dando, forming andando rather than an incomplete word.

The damaged beginning completes andando; the lower remains of d support restoring it. The next examples are ki no ne ga nuketa and, across the line break, faremono no ne ga nuketa: a tree's root or the core of a swelling coming out.

This completes faremonono nega nuqeta. The Portuguese begins “the root comes out,” covering both the literal root and the core of a swelling; printed f represents the historical Japanese h-series pronunciation.
The root belongs to a tree or, figuratively, to a swelling. Daruore and dalgum are retained contractions in the original Portuguese.

runs.text: O comprar algũa couſa às escondi-

lines.note: Nuqegai is clandestine buying outside the normal trading arrangement. The scan reads couſa and escondi-, not the OCR's bouſa and es cendi-; the latter continues as das below.

runs.text: das fora da armação, ou peço corrente.

lines.note: The purchase is outside the trading arrangement or current price. The scan's weak word is retained as peço, as in the supplied transcription, rather than silently inserting an uncertain r to normalize it to preço.

Nuqegai or nuqevri o suru means to buy or sell in this clandestine way; the Portuguese continues at the top of column 2. The OCR omitted nuqevriuo ſuru and the translation. The damaged printed Coprar is retained without supplying an unverified nasal mark.

runs.text: ou vender algũa couſa deſta maneira.

lines.note: This completes the bottom of column 1: “buy or sell something in this way,” namely clandestinely outside the usual trading arrangement. The column transition is continuous, with no missing intervening row.

runs.text: Pelle, ou caſca de cegarrega, ou

lines.note: Nuqegara, nukegara, is a shed skin or shell. The first example is a cicada; the damaged Portuguese cegarrega retains a visible descending remnant of its second g, where the OCR substituted punctuation. The headword's weak second letter is u.

runs.text: de outro qualquer bicho, que porſi tira, ou deſ-

lines.note: Any other creature's shed covering is included: the creature removes or casts it off itself. The verb is tira, not the OCR's tura, and deſ- joins pede below.
This completes deſpede do corpo, “casts off from the body,” finishing the shed-skin definition. It is not the unrelated verb pede in isolation.
Nuqenuqeni means secretly or by slipping away unobtrusively. Adu. identifies an adverb and Vt introduces the following example.

The example refers to warriors in the capital and outlying districts coming secretly. The scan has Racuchǔ fendono buximo without the OCR's period after Racuchǔ; the caron belongs to the long final vowel of rakuchu.
Mairu completes the Japanese sentence. The source citation is Tai., book 29, not the OCR's n9; the Portuguese translation begins “the soldiers from within,” with dẽ- continuing below.

runs.text: tro do Miaco, & dos confins vinhão eſcondi-

lines.note: The soldiers are from Miyako and the border districts and came secretly. Miaco is the embedded Japanese place designation; eſcondi- continues as damente below.
The soldiers came secretly, little by little. This completes the adverbial example and its Portuguese translation.
Nuqetouori, nuketooru, means to pass through from one side to another. The printed touori spelling and its ru, otta inflections are retained.
The alternative Portuguese wording is “to be pierced through.” This completes the same entry rather than adding another headword or changing the Japanese inflection.
Nuqevri, nukeuri, cross-refers to Nuqegai, where clandestine buying and selling were treated together. Nuqegai here is an embedded Japanese reference after Vide.

runs.text: Paos como ripas que atraueſão de co-

lines.note: This noun Nuqi denotes horizontal timbers or ties resembling laths. The Portuguese starts to explain that they run from one column to another; co- belongs to colũna.
The timbers run between wooden columns. The two colũna forms retain the printed nasal abbreviation and complete the constructional definition.
The verb Nuqi, nuku, means to pull or take out. A series of examples begins with Ca-, continued as catanauo nuqu on the next row; this is not the preceding architectural noun.
Catanauo nuqu means to draw a sword. The second Catana is inside the Portuguese translation; the first belongs to the Japanese example split across rows.
Manacouo nuqu illustrates pulling out the eyes. The example is Japanese, followed by its Portuguese translation; the historical manaco spelling is retained.
Yauo nuqu means to pull out an arrow. The printed mark over the final a in està is a grave, not a nasal tilde, and there is no full stop before the continuation describing the embedded arrow.
The arrow is stuck or lodged in something. The next example, qeuo nuqu, concerns plucking hair, and its Portuguese verb Ar- continues below.
The first phrase completes “pull out the hairs.” Cuguiuo nuqu then introduces pulling out nails; it belongs to the same series of examples for nuku.
The translation explains removing nails. The next example, axiuo nuqu, begins the sense of extracting one's foot and is split after nu-.

runs.text: Tirar o pee como da neue, ou lama,

lines.note: Axiuo nuqu means to pull the foot out, as from snow or mud. Pee and neue are retained historical Portuguese spellings.
The foot is being withdrawn from where it became stuck. A fuller example begins with snow reaching to the chest; a- starts atarimade across the line break.
The person has sunk into snow up to the chest and tries to pull the feet out. Nucanto is the intended-action form of nuku; ſure- continues into the concessive ſuredomo below.

The sentence ends “although he tried, he could not.” The citation is id., book 18, not iô; id. refers back to the previously named work. The Portuguese begins with the printed Acaruando-, describing becoming stuck.

runs.text: ſe na neue tè os peitos poſto que fazia por ar-

lines.note: Having sunk in snow as far as the chest, the person tried to pull free. Tè retains its printed grave accent, and ar- joins rancar below.
Despite trying, the person could not pull out the feet. The scan reads podia, with i rather than the OCR's t in podta.
This separate Nuqi entry gives the figurative sense “deceive.” It has the same inflectional endings as the preceding physical extraction verb but is independently set as a headword.
Nuqiauaxe means to draw together or in mutual opposition. The historical ſuru ending is retained; juntamẽ- continues the Portuguese adverb below.
The example has two people drawing swords against one another. The separated nuqi auaſuru is retained as printed rather than joined into a modern normalized form.

runs.text: Arrancarem dous hũ contra outro as catanas.

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly says that two people draw their swords, one against the other. Catanas is a Japanese loanword embedded in this translation.

runs.text: O ir manſamente pee ante pee co-

lines.note: Nuqiaxi means stepping quietly or stealthily, one foot after another. Both occurrences are printed pee; the second is not the OCR's shortened pe. Co- continues as como below.

The quiet stepping is described as fearful. The example begins with crouching or lowering oneself before heaven; xe is the dictionary's historical spelling, not a reason to alter the text to modern se.
The parallel phrase concerns treading cautiously on the earth. The Portuguese renders the preceding clause as lowering one's head before heaven; the spacing nuqi axiſu is retained.

runs.text: & piſar a terra com medo, & reuerencia.

lines.note: The second clause is translated as treading the earth with fear and reverence. This completes the paired example rather than defining a new religious term.
Nuqicaqe, nukikakeru, means to begin drawing or draw a little. The following row specifies a partly drawn sword.
The alternative wording describes drawing the sword halfway. Mea is retained as the printed historical form; it is not expanded to modern meia.
Nuqi cutçurogue means to loosen or partly draw the sword. The final Portuguese word is visibly hũ, with a nasal abbreviation, not the OCR's hi; the separated headword elements are retained.
This completes “draw the sword a little,” specifying the limited action meant by Nuqi cutçurogue.
Nuqifanaxi, nukihanasu, means to draw completely, with an alternative forceful sense continued below. The printed historical aita past form is retained.
The alternative sense is drawing the sword forcefully. Catana is embedded in the Portuguese explanation, not a standalone Japanese example.
Nuqigaqi, nukigaki, is an extract or compilation. Nu- begins the corresponding verbal example on the next row; Cõpendio retains its nasal abbreviation.
Nuqigaqiuo ſuru means to make extracts or a compilation from a book. Algũ retains the printed nasal mark, and the example remains roman while its translation is italic.
Nuqijiro names a kind of textile or piece-goods. The Portuguese gives only this broad description, so a precise fabric identification is not inserted into the canonical text.

Nuqiidaxi, nukiidasu, first means to pull out. The second scan pass and enlargement confirm two separate dotted i letters between q and d; the OCR's Nuqidaxi omitted one. Item introduces the further extract-or-compile sense below, and the historical aita inflection is preserved.

runs.text: Recopilar. Mas não ſe vſa na pratica.

lines.note: The second sense is to compile or excerpt, with a warning that this is not used in ordinary speech. The restriction belongs to this lexical sense rather than the whole page.

Nuqijrede describes the hands placed inside the sleeves. The scan reads das at the row end, not the OCR's da-; the separate right-aligned italic mangas. below supplies the catchword for the continuation.
This right-aligned word is printed below the last ordinary body row as the catchword; it continues the unfinished phrase about hands inside the sleeves. The italic word and its period are retained.
